article_title: The Role of Selective High Schools in Equalizing Educational Outcomes
citation: Allensworth, E., Moore, P., Sartain, L., & de la Torre, M. (2016). The Educational Benefits of Attending Higher-Performing Schools: Evidence from Chicago High Schools. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications
title: Two companion studies using propensity score and regression discontinuity designs
description: The summary rests on two studies. The first examines "the effects of attending a higher-performing school on students' academic and nonacademic outcomes" using "a propensity score approach with an extensive array of pre-high school characteristics" for CPS cohorts entering high school from 2008-2011. The second compares students just above and just below selective enrollment admission thresholds in a regression discontinuity design for 2010-2013 cohorts, investigating neighborhood socioeconomic differences.
requirements: Comparisons match students on prior test scores, grades, attendance, and family and middle school characteristics
constraints: Findings are average effects for Chicago Public Schools students in the studied cohorts and may not generalize beyond them
target_learners: first-time ninth-graders in Chicago Public Schools
target_learning_goals: high school achievement, student experiences, and college outcomes
examples: The threshold comparison studies students from neighborhoods with low and high socioeconomic status (tier 1, tier 4)
key_sources: Allensworth, E., Moore, P., Sartain, L., & de la Torre, M. (2016). The Educational Benefits of Attending Higher-Performing Schools: Evidence from Chicago High Schools. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications

article_title: UCLA Community School: Celebrating Language, Culture, and Community
citation: Karen Hunter Quartz. (2023). UCLA Community School: Celebrating Language, Culture, and Community. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org
title: Four core competencies and three core beliefs guiding teaching and learning at UCLA-CS
description: UCLA-CS grounds instruction in three core beliefs, including that "Language and culture are central to learning and human development", and in four core student competencies developed with multiple stakeholders: becoming a self-directed, passionate learner; a master of academic content and skills; an individual who is bilingual, biliterate, and multicultural; and an active and critical participant in society. The competencies drive annual inquiry and improvement and, the report says, guard against narrowing of the curriculum.
requirements: Stakeholder collaboration during school design to articulate the competencies
target_learners: All TK-12 students and adult members of the school community
examples: Teachers evaluated Multilingual Interdisciplinary Social Action projects with a rubric aligned with the four core competencies
key_sources: Karen Hunter Quartz. (2023). UCLA Community School: Celebrating Language, Culture, and Community. Learning Policy Institute. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED642538

article_title: UCLA Community School: Celebrating Language, Culture, and Community
citation: Karen Hunter Quartz. (2023). UCLA Community School: Celebrating Language, Culture, and Community. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org
title: Dual-language program and Reader Identity Self-Assessment for biliteracy development
description: UCLA-CS is a dual-language school offering content instruction in Spanish, Korean, and English, with elementary Spanish-English and Korean-English programs and a Grades 9-12 Spanish pathway; about 4 in 10 students earn the California State Seal of Biliteracy. Students in Grades 2-5 take the Reader Identity Self-Assessment (RISA) each fall, analyzing their Spanish and English reading data, setting goals, and reflecting on their "bilingual or multilingual reader selves", then tracking progress in longitudinal bar graphs shared with families.
requirements: Classroom-developed and standardized assessments to capture biliteracy development
parent-teacher conferences where students share reading plans and reflections
constraints: The Korean-English program allocates one day each week to Korean, an approach developed with Korean-speaking parents and caregivers
target_learners: Elementary through high school emergent bilingual students
examples: A 4th-grader set a goal to learn more Spanish vocabulary and read with stamina, then reflected on progress each spring
key_sources: Karen Hunter Quartz. (2023). UCLA Community School: Celebrating Language, Culture, and Community. Learning Policy Institute. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED642538

article_title: Community Schools Certification: An Approach for Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Maier, A., Espinoza, D., & Oakes, J. (2025). Community schools certification: An approach for implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/220.412
title: University of Central Florida Center for Community Schools certification system for the Community Partnership Schools model
description: The UCF Center houses a state-funded certification process for the Community Partnership Schools (CPS) model throughout Florida, based on 12 standards with substandards divided into nonnegotiable "fundamental practices" and an overall assessment scored on a four-point rubric. Schools apply once key partnerships and positions are filled, then spend up to 5 years self-assessing, gathering artifacts, and receiving "technical assistance, coaching, and peer-to-peer mentoring" before a readiness assessment and a 3-day external review. In fiscal year 2024, $20.1 million in state funding was appropriated to UCF Center, which currently serves 43 schools.
requirements: Schools must have a memorandum of understanding with each of the four required core partners (nonprofit agency, university/college, school district, and health care provider), the director position in place, and programming aligned with community needs.
constraints: The model requires certain staffing and features to be in place, which can limit who and how many schools can participate in certification; some participants felt the standards were too rigid or difficult to achieve in their context and the data collection process was cumbersome.
target_learners: K-12 students in Florida Community Partnership Schools
target_learning_goals: implementation fidelity of the community schools strategy
examples: Planning grants are awarded for up to $80,000 with a 25% match; implementation grants typically range from $150,000 to $200,000 per year for the first 5 years.
key_sources: Germain, E., Maier, A., Espinoza, D., & Oakes, J. (2025). Community schools certification: An approach for implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/220.412

article_title: Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators through Teacher Residencies
citation: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797
title: UCLA IMPACT ECE/Multiple Subject Program
description: A social justice–focused urban teacher residency run by LAUSD and UCLA Center X (2010–2014), through which candidates earned a Child Development Master Teacher Permit, Multiple Subject certification, and a Master of Education degree in 18 months. It began with a weeklong institute on child development and inclusion, required the eight early childhood core courses (the CAP 8) for the child development permit, and included extensive clinical placements in early childhood settings (6 hours a day, 4 days a week) and elementary classrooms (approximately 30 hours per week). Residents received a $10,000 fellowship; mentors received a $3,000 stipend and monthly "Methods With Mentors" professional development organized around UCLA's five dimensions of mentoring quality.
requirements: Completion of the CAP 8 early childhood core courses for the child development permit
Mentor selection and matching based on effective teaching and program values
constraints: The program required a large number of courses because residents pursued two certifications and a master's degree; the director noted integrating ECE and multiple subject courses would be a value add
target_learners: Candidates interested in early childhood education in traditionally underserved urban communities
target_learning_goals: Child development expertise, developmentally appropriate practice, social justice–oriented instruction, and inquiry-based reflective practice
examples: Residents' inquiries addressed puzzles of practice such as creating environments in which families feel welcome, differentiating instruction, and implementing classroom management strategies.
key_sources: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797

article_title: On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging
citation: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2
title: UCLA Migrant Student Leadership Institute as a third space
description: The MSLI is presented as an illustrative example of a third space—an approach or zone of development that transforms 'conflict and difference into rich zones of collaboration and learning.' It reorganized educational practices so that college-bound students of color from migrant farmworker backgrounds could see themselves as learners and social change agents, drawing on rigorous texts, mini-lectures, discussions, writing and reading conferences, field trips, theater, and college preparation workshops, and connecting students' community histories to present-day realities.
requirements: Organizers must work outside pre-existing conventions of what a learning space and its tools are
constraints: The third space emerges from the collision of official and unofficial scripts; redirecting students back to the official curriculum thwarts its transformative potential
target_learners: college-bound students of color from migrant farmworker backgrounds
target_learning_goals: critical inquiry, seeing oneself as a learner and social change agent, and revising constructions of self, community, and schooling
examples: Students used traditional tools such as dictionaries and conventional writing rules in new ways to reflect on, contest, and revise their constructions of themselves and their schooling experiences
key_sources: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2

article_title: Profiles of mathematical deficits in children with dyslexia
citation: B. Pedemonte, C. W. Pereira, V. Borghesani, M. Ebbert, I. E. Allen, P. Pinheiro-Chagas, J. De Leon, Z. Miller, B. L. Tee & M. L. Gorno-Tempini. (2024). Profiles of mathematical deficits in children with dyslexia. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00217-x
title: UCSF Mathematical Cognition Battery (MCB)
description: The UCSF MCB is an experimental battery developed at the UCSF Dyslexia Center to identify and differentiate mathematical difficulties in children with dyslexia. "It spans number processing, arithmeti cal procedures, arithmetic facts retrieval, and geometrical abilities, allowing for personalized educational practices and interventions based on individual proﬁles." It has seven grade-specific forms for grades 2–8 and "encompasses a total of 19 subtests, including 4 computer-based subtests and 15 paper-based subtests", plus subtests for complex skills and teaching exposure, with completion times recorded to assess fluency.
requirements: Administration with recording of both accuracy and completion time; grade-appropriate form selection
constraints: The MCB has not yet been standardized; criteria currently rely on clinical and qualitative evaluations, and some subtests may be redundant or unnecessary
target_learners: children in grades 2–8 referred for dyslexia evaluation
target_learning_goals: identifying individual mathematical strengths and weaknesses across four domains
key_sources: B. Pedemonte, C. W. Pereira, V. Borghesani, M. Ebbert, I. E. Allen, P. Pinheiro-Chagas, J. De Leon, Z. Miller, B. L. Tee & M. L. Gorno-Tempini. (2024). Profiles of mathematical deficits in children with dyslexia. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00217-x

article_title: Enhancing ICU-OR Handoff Communication Through Simulation-Based Education in Nurse Anesthesiology Training.
citation: Meyers AB, Morgan B, Smallheer B. (2026). Enhancing ICU-OR Handoff Communication Through Simulation-Based Education in Nurse Anesthesiology Training. Critical Care Nursing Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1097/CNQ.0000000000000627
title: UCLA OR-to-ICU Bedside Handoff Checklist Tool adapted for a simulation-based ICU-OR handoff training scenario
description: A structured handoff communication tool adapted from the UCLA OR-to-ICU Bedside Handoff Checklist Tool, organizing the handoff into 4 sequential phases: introduction, surgeon report, anesthesia report, and critical care team readback. It prompts systematic communication of patient identifiers, neurologic and hemodynamic status, ventilator settings, current infusions with weight verification, procedural details, postoperative management parameters, line/drain/tube placements, and anticipated clinical concerns. It concludes with a structured readback component requiring the receiving team to summarize the immediate plan of care, prioritize clinical concerns, and confirm contact information and call triggers, thereby closing the communication loop.
requirements: Used within a simulation-based education context to allow students to practice and refine systematic handoff communication before encountering critical scenarios in clinical practice.
constraints: The article notes this type of handoff tool has been shown to reduce information omissions, minimize reliance on memory, and create a shared cognitive model among interdisciplinary team members during high-risk care transitions.
target_learning_goals: Standardized handoff communication during ICU-OR care transitions
Interprofessional communication and team-based care processes
examples: Used in a high-fidelity simulation of a 28-year-old male trauma patient status post gunshot wound requiring return to the OR for re-exploration and washout.
key_sources: Meyers AB, Morgan B, Smallheer B. (2026). Enhancing ICU-OR Handoff Communication Through Simulation-Based Education in Nurse Anesthesiology Training. Critical Care Nursing Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1097/CNQ.0000000000000627

article_title: Developing a psychosocial competency framework for adult and older adult acute mental health inpatient care.
citation: Wood, L., Williams, C., Luxon, L., Kumary, A., & Roth, A. (2025). Developing a psychosocial competency framework for adult and older adult acute mental health inpatient care. Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice, 98, 553–569. https://doi.org/10.1111/papt.12575
title: Interactive online competence map hosted on the UCL competency framework website
description: The framework is published as an interactive online 'map' on the UCL competency framework website, giving an overview of key areas of knowledge, skills and attitudes. The article states "The map is designed to be viewed online in an interactive format so that each competency can be linked to a further list of more detailed competences", allowing users to drill down from broad areas to specific competence items. The full list of competences is freely available as an open-access document.
requirements: Online hosting so each competency can link to a more detailed list of competences
target_learners: Trainers and supervisors in acute mental health care
target_learning_goals: Understanding which competences are needed for high-quality acute inpatient care
examples: The map and full competence list are available at the UCL competency framework website cited in the Results section
key_sources: Wood, L., Williams, C., Luxon, L., Kumary, A., & Roth, A. (2025). Developing a psychosocial competency framework for adult and older adult acute mental health inpatient care. Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice, 98, 553–569. https://doi.org/10.1111/papt.12575

article_title: Digital and artificial intelligence-assisted cephalometric training effectively enhanced students' landmarking accuracy in preclinical orthodontic education.
citation: Lin Jiayu, Liao Zhihao, Dai Jingtao, Wang Manyi, Yu Ruixue, Yang Hong, Liu Chufeng. (2025). Digital and artificial intelligence-assisted cephalometric training effectively enhanced students’ landmarking accuracy in preclinical orthodontic education. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-025-05978-4
title: Uceph digital cephalometric training software with scored landmarking and visual error correction
description: A digital cephalometric training platform (Uceph, Chengdu, China) used for both assessment and practice in preclinical orthodontic education. The software "included preloaded lateral radiographs with predefined “correct positions” for various landmark points" and assigned scores of 0–10 per landmark based on distance from the correct position. Its training mode visually indicates correct landmark positions with a circle, letting students adjust until close to the correct answer, and it generates total scores before and after training.
requirements: Preloaded lateral radiographs with predefined correct landmark positions
A scoring system based on distance between the selected point and the correct position
target_learning_goals: accurate identification of cephalometric landmarks on lateral radiographs
examples: Forty undergraduates in pairs measured two lateral radiographs before and after training, with total scores recorded for comparison.
key_sources: Lin Jiayu, Liao Zhihao, Dai Jingtao, Wang Manyi, Yu Ruixue, Yang Hong, Liu Chufeng. (2025). Digital and artificial intelligence-assisted cephalometric training effectively enhanced students’ landmarking accuracy in preclinical orthodontic education. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-025-05978-4

article_title: Relationships between preadmission variables and academic outcomes for postbaccalaureate students in medical school.
citation: Schneid Stephen D., Kelly Carolyn J., Brandl Katharina. (2022). Relationships between preadmission variables and academic outcomes for postbaccalaureate students in medical school. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-022-10129-3
title: UCSD PBPM program: a yearlong, 48-unit academic record enhancer postbaccalaureate program
description: The UCSD Extension PBPM program, launched in 2013 in partnership with the School of Medicine and Division of Biological Sciences, is a "yearlong, 48-unit program" for applicants who have already completed prerequisite coursework. Students take upper-division biomedical science courses plus cohort-only advanced courses with frequent testing and feedback, MCAT preparation support, faculty advising, and a mock multiple mini interview. The article evaluates its alumni's medical school outcomes.
requirements: Students must have already completed their premedical prerequisite coursework
constraints: It is an academic record enhancer type program, distinct from career-changer programs with heterogeneous curricula
target_learners: first-time applicants and re-applicants to medical schools seeking to strengthen their academic record
target_learning_goals: building a strong biomedical science foundation for medical school coursework
examples: Students take three courses during summer, fall, winter, and spring quarters, including upper division Physiology, Endocrinology, Pharmacology, Cell Biology, Immunology, Molecular Biology, Genetics, and Biochemistry
key_sources: Schneid Stephen D., Kelly Carolyn J., Brandl Katharina. (2022). Relationships between preadmission variables and academic outcomes for postbaccalaureate students in medical school. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-022-10129-3

article_title: Multi-Layer Perception model with Elastic Grey Wolf Optimization to predict student achievement.
citation: Song Yinqiu, Meng Xianqiu, Jiang Jianhua. (2022). Multi-Layer Perception model with Elastic Grey Wolf Optimization to predict student achievement. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0276943
title: UCI Student Performance dataset (two Portuguese secondary schools)
description: The study uses the student performance dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, collected "through reports and questionnaires on the performance of students in secondary education" in two Portuguese schools. "The dataset contains thirty attributes", including demographic, social, and school-related characteristics and family features, with two subject datasets (Mathematics and Portuguese). The thirty attributes are the input of the prediction model, and the article sets 80% training data and 20% testing data.
requirements: Attributes span school, sex, age, family size, parents' education and jobs, study time, failures, support, alcohol consumption, health, and absences
constraints: The article notes a limitation: the amount of data and feature attributes in existence referencing the UCI data influences prediction accuracy
target_learners: secondary education students in two Portuguese schools
target_learning_goals: predicting student achievement in Mathematics and Portuguese
examples: Descriptive analysis reports 53% girls, most students in city home addresses, 69% of guardians are mothers, and service workers reach 26% for father and 26% for mother
key_sources: Song Yinqiu, Meng Xianqiu, Jiang Jianhua. (2022). Multi-Layer Perception model with Elastic Grey Wolf Optimization to predict student achievement. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0276943
